identity.title: FAUST. X. Formaldehyde in the protobinary system [BHB2007] 11: Small-scale deuteration

paper_type_evidence.quote: We observed the Class 0/I protobinary system [BHB2007] 11, whose emission components are embedded in circumstellar disks that have radii of 2 to 3 au, using the Atacama Large Millimeter Array (ALMA) within the context of the Large Program Fifty AU STudy of the chemistry in the disk/envelope system of Solar-like protostars (FAUST).
Within the context of the Large Program FAUST, the Class 0/I protostellar core [BHB2007] 11 was observed in the ALMA large project 2018.1.01205.L between 2018 and 2020

evidence.quote: [BHB2007] 11 is a Class 0/I protostellar core ((cite: brooke), (cite: forbrich), (cite: sandell)) located 163 $\pm$ 5 pc away ((cite: dzib)) in the Barnard 59 (B59) core.
This object has a bolometric temperature of 60-70 K, luminosity of 2.2-4.5 L$_\odot$ and systemic velocity of 3.6 km s$^{-1}$ ((cite: onishi), (cite: brooke), (cite: forbrich), (cite: sandell)).

Previous observations have revealed [BHB2007] 11 as a protobinary system with two central objects (hereafter denoted A ($\alpha$(2000)=17h11m23.1058s, $\delta$(2000)=-27’32.828") and B ($\alpha$(2000)=17h11m23.1015s, $\delta$(2000)=-27’33.987"), respectively, located approximately 28 au apart (in projection) with A to the north of B ((cite: alves_19)).

question.value: Constrain the deuterium fractionation ratios in formaldehyde (H2CO, HDCO, and D2CO) at small spatial scales in the Class 0/I protobinary system [BHB2007] 11 and investigate the kinematics of its extended emission.

evidence.quote: We aim to constrain the deuterium fractionation ratios in a Class 0/I protostellar object in formaldehyde (H$_2$CO), which has abundant deuterated isotopologues in this environment.
In addition, based on the kinematics seen in the observations of the H$_2$CO emission, we propose the presence of a second large scale outflow.
Within the context of the Large Program FAUST, the Class 0/I protostellar core [BHB2007] 11 was observed in the ALMA large project 2018.1.01205.L between 2018 and 2020
This paper makes use of the following ALMA data: ADS/JAO.ALMA2018.1.01205.L.

evidence.quote: The clean maps were analysed with the GILDAS software. The line channels were identified and used to create moment 0 maps for each of the transitions.
For the analysis of all lines in our sample, the 4$\sigma$ contour (the minimum to define a detection) of the map of the HDCO transition at 259 GHz was used to define a polygon for extraction.

The spectra of the four transitions were extracted in flux density units (S$_\nu$) within the aforementioned polygon; these were converted to synthesised beam temperature units (K) in the GILDAS package CLASS using conversion factors calculated using Eq.

analysis_steps.goal: Measure emitting component sizes via 2D image deconvolution

method.value: Run 2D Gaussian deconvolution on the peak emission channel of each of the three velocity components in both HDCO transitions (excluding the blended component of HDCO 4(1,4)-3(1,3)) using CASA imfit.

evidence.quote: In order to check this assumption, we ran a 2D deconvolution of all three emission components in both HDCO transitions (with the exception of the blended component of the HDCO 4(1,4)-3(1,3) transition) applying the CASA *imfit* command to the peak emission channel in each case.

The results of this deconvolution returned image component size estimates (major axis FWHM x minor axis FWHM) of 0.34" $\times$ 0.27" for the component at approximately -1 km s$^{-1}$, 1.37" $\times$ 0.68" for the component at approximately 3 km s$^{-1}$ and 0.30" $\times$ 0.20" for the component at approximately 9 km s$^{-1}$.

analysis_steps.goal: Perform LTE radiative transfer modelling and derive column densities and D/H ratios

method.value: Fit Gaussian line profiles using Levenberg-Marquardt fitting and perform LTE radiative transfer MCMC modelling in CASSIS to derive V_LSR, FWHM, T_ex, and total column densities (N_TOT) for HDCO, H2CO, and D2CO, then compute D/H = 0.5 * N(HDCO)/N(H2CO).

evidence.quote: The molecular column densities have been derived assuming Local Thermodynamic Equilibrium (LTE) conditions. Therefore, we can utilise equations from the Formalism for CASSIS Software

Within CASSIS, we used constraints provided by our initial Gaussian fitting in order to obtain best fit values for FWHM, V$_{\rm LSR}$, $T_{\rm ex}$ and $N_{\rm TOT}$ of our two unblended components at $\sim$ -1 and $\sim$ 3 km s$^{-1}$ using Monte Carlo Markov-Chain (MCMC) fitting, assuming a 10% calibration error.

key_parameters.value: Emitting sizes for beam dilution correction: lower limit 0.15" (Source B) and 0.50" (Source A); upper limit 0.30" (Source B) and 1.00" (Source A)

evidence.quote: we therefore ran two LTE radiative transfer analyses, one assuming a lower limit emitting size of 0.15" (for the components associated with Source B) and 0.50" (for the Source A component) and the other assuming an upper limit emission area of 0.30" (for the components associated with Source B) and 1.00" (for the Source A component).

key_parameters.value: Fixed T_ex = 90 K for H2CO and D2CO emission components (and blended HDCO component); T_ex = 13 K (or <13 K) for envelope absorption

evidence.quote: Therefore, using a fixed $T_{\rm ex}$ of 90 K and our best fit V$_{\rm LSR}$ and FWHM values from HDCO, we constrained Gaussian fits for each of the three emission components visible in the H$_2$CO spectrum.

To achieve this, we added a value for the continuum of 10.3 K from our observations and assumed an excitation temperature of 13 K to simulate the temperature of the cold envelope in which the absorption was occurring.

Therefore, we used LTE analysis with the aforementioned V$_{\rm LSR}$ and FWHM values, an assumed excitation temperature of 90 K and an upper limit emitting size of both 0.3" (covering Source B emission) and 1.0" (covering Source A emission) to obtain upper limit values of N$_{\rm TOT}$ for the single D$_2$CO component.

validation.value: Calculated 3-sigma integrated intensity upper limit (0.36 K km s^-1) to verify the 7-sigma detection of the weak D2CO line (0.826 K km s^-1); checked line blending with CH3OCHO in CASSIS using E_u <= 150 K.

evidence.quote: The line identification software in CASSIS was used to check the transitions that could potentially cause this blending; based on the Einstein coefficients and $E_{\rm u}$ (upper energy level - using a maximum value of 150 K), the most likely culprit is CH$_3$OCHO 19(4,15)-18(4,14) A

The integrated intensity of our D$_2$CO line is 0.826 K km s$^{-1}$, therefore yielding a ratio of 2.3 compared to the 3$\sigma$ threshold. Thus, our D$_2$CO observations have a s/n ratio of approximately 7$\sigma$ in integrated intensity.

analysis_steps.goal: Map centroid velocities and model extended kinematics with a free-fall streamer model

method.value: Perform pixel-by-pixel Gaussian fitting on H2CO (between 0 and 6 km s^-1, split at 3.5 km s^-1) using pyspeckit for pixels >= 5-sigma, define polygons excluding high-velocity disk emission, and compare sky trajectories and velocity-distance profiles against an analytic free-falling streamline model.

findings_qualitative.value: Undeuterated H2CO is ubiquitous across both the compact disk and extended envelope, whereas deuterated HDCO and D2CO are confined to the central circumstellar disk region within ~300 au.

evidence.quote: From our ALMA observations, our results agree with current literature in only finding the deuterated species HDCO and D$_2$CO in the central regions of the core, while undeuterated H$_2$CO is found more ubiquitously.

It is clear from these spectra that, while the H$_2$CO emission is extended, the HDCO emission is compact and not seen in any of the spectra outside that extracted from the central pixel; indeed, HDCO is only seen within $\sim$ 300 au of the centre.

findings_qualitative.value: H2CO and HDCO spectra display three velocity components consistent with CH3OH hotspots: two high-velocity components originating near Source B and one central velocity component near Source A.

evidence.quote: Radiative transfer analysis has shown that there are three velocity components associated with both deuterated and undeuterated formaldehyde in this source, consistent with other FAUST observations. The velocity values of these components are consistent with the conclusion that the two components showing strong redshift and blueshift are originating from the southern Source B and the low velocity component is originating from the northern Source A, again consistent with other organic species.

findings_qualitative.value: H2CO exhibits a central absorption feature between ~2 and 5 km s^-1 caused by cold foreground envelope gas within ~500 au of the dust peak.

evidence.quote: Additionally, H$_2$CO exhibits an absorption feature ($\sim$ 2 to 5 km s$^{-1}$) due to absorption in the cold envelope of emission originating from warm inner regions, which, according to pixel-by-pixel analysis, is seen in a circular region that extends to approximately 500 au from the centre and is centred on the dust peak.

findings_qualitative.value: Extended low-velocity H2CO emission traces a large-scale dynamic structure perpendicular to the known CO 2-1 outflow; kinematic modelling shows it is inconsistent with an infalling streamer and tentatively identifies it as a second, asymmetric molecular outflow driven by a wide-angle disk wind.

evidence.quote: Following the results of kinematic modelling, the second large scale feature appears to be inconsistent with a streamer-like nature due to a flat and outflowing velocity relation; we thus tentatively conclude that the feature is an asymmetric molecular outflow launched by a wide-angle disk wind.

claims.hypothesis: Deuterated formaldehyde (HDCO and D2CO) in the Class 0/I protobinary [BHB2007] 11 is spatially compact and shares the shocked circumstellar disk origin of CH3OH, whereas undeuterated H2CO is extended across the core and envelope.
claims.experiment: Combined 12 m and 7 m ALMA Band 6 observations from the FAUST Large Program to map H2CO 3(0,3)-2(0,2), HDCO 4(1,4)-3(1,3), HDCO 4(2,2)-3(2,1), and D2CO 4(0,4)-3(0,3), and extracted multi-component spectra and pixel-by-pixel spectra.
claims.result: H2CO is detected throughout the disk and envelope (with foreground envelope absorption inside ~500 au), while HDCO and D2CO are only detected in the central region (<300 au), showing three velocity components (-1.2, 3.4, and 9-10 km s^-1) in H2CO and HDCO matching previously identified CH3OH components.
claims.finding: HDCO and D2CO originate only from the compact circumstellar disk/shocked regions near Sources A and B, while undeuterated H2CO traces both the inner disk and extended envelope.

evidence.quote: From our ALMA observations, our results agree with current literature in only finding the deuterated species HDCO and D$_2$CO in the central regions of the core, while undeuterated H$_2$CO is found more ubiquitously.

indeed, HDCO is only seen within $\sim$ 300 au of the centre. From this, we postulate that HDCO likely originates from the shocked regions first identified in (cite: vastel) located to both sides of Source B and also near Source A.

claims.hypothesis: The deuterium fractionation (D/H ratio) of formaldehyde in [BHB2007] 11 is enhanced relative to the cosmic ratio and comparable to other low-mass Class 0/I protobinary systems.
claims.experiment: Performed LTE radiative transfer modelling (Levenberg-Marquardt and MCMC fitting in CASSIS) of the extracted H2CO, HDCO, and D2CO spectra, correcting for beam dilution using CASA imfit 2D deconvolved sizes.
claims.result: Derived column densities of (3-8) x 10^14 cm^-2 for H2CO, (0.8-2.9) x 10^13 cm^-2 for HDCO, and (2.6-4.3) x 10^12 cm^-2 for D2CO, yielding an average D/H ratio from HDCO of 0.02 (+0.02/-0.01).
claims.finding: The formaldehyde D/H ratio in [BHB2007] 11 is ~0.02 (upper limit due to assumed uniform H2CO emission), which is lower than in several other star-forming regions but consistent within uncertainties with the protobinary IRAS 16293-2422 B (0.03 +/- 0.01); D/H from D2CO cannot be reliably constrained due to an ambiguous velocity shift.

evidence.quote: From the radiative transfer modelling, the column density of H$_2$CO ranges between (3-8)$\times$10$^{14}$ cm$^{-2}$ and that of HDCO ranges between (0.8-2.9)$\times$10$^{13}$ cm$^{-2}$. Column density for the single detected velocity component of D$_2$CO ranges between (2.6-4.3)$\times$10$^{12}$ cm$^{-2}$. This yields an average D/H ratio for formaldehyde in [BHB2007] 11 of 0.02$^{+0.02}_{-0.01}$ from HDCO .
For comparison, (cite: persson) found a D/H ratio of 0.03$\pm$0.01 in HDCO towards the protobinary IRAS16293-2422 B, within uncertainty of the value found in the present work towards [BHB2007] 11.

claims.hypothesis: The newly detected large-scale (~2000 au) dynamic H2CO emission feature oriented perpendicular to the known CO 2-1 outflow is an infalling accretion streamer.
claims.experiment: Fitted pixel-by-pixel Gaussian centroids above 5-sigma with pyspeckit and modelled the sky trajectory and velocity-distance profile of the redshifted and blueshifted lobes using an analytic free-fall streamline model.
claims.result: While the plane-of-sky trajectory can be matched, the velocity-distance relation is flat in the redshifted lobe and slightly outward-moving in the blueshifted lobe, lacking the inward acceleration of free-falling gas.
claims.finding: The extended dynamic feature is inconsistent with an infalling streamer and is tentatively proposed to be a second, asymmetric molecular outflow launched by a wide-angle disk wind.

evidence.quote: Following the results of kinematic modelling, the second large scale feature appears to be inconsistent with a streamer-like nature due to a flat and outflowing velocity relation; we thus tentatively conclude that the feature is an asymmetric molecular outflow launched by a wide-angle disk wind.

However, due to a lack of a clear acceleration or deceleration, as well as a velocity relation that is flat or even outflowing, this investigation instead led to the conclusion that the feature is most likely not streamer-like in nature and, in fact, is most likely a second molecular outflow

why_this_data.value: Interferometric observations combining multiple ALMA 12 m and 7 m configurations within FAUST probe both small (~50 au disk) and large (envelope) scales simultaneously in a spectral setup covering multiple deuterated species in the understudied Class 0/I protobinary [BHB2007] 11.

evidence.quote: Interferometric observations are therefore required to probe deeper into protostellar objects and reveal the chemistry within. In particular, the object of this study, [BHB2007] 11, is very understudied compared to other similar sources
Additionally, observing the core with multiple configurations enables both large- and small-scale analysis of our source.

why_this_method.value: The 4-sigma contour of HDCO 259 GHz was chosen to define the extraction polygon because it is detected at 8-sigma and is free from the CH3OCHO blending affecting the 246 GHz line; a 5-sigma threshold and 0-6 km s^-1 velocity window were chosen for centroid velocity maps to isolate dynamic extended emission without dilution.

evidence.quote: This transition was chosen to estimate the D/H ratio because it is detected at a signal-to-noise ratio (s/n) of 8$\sigma$ and because the HDCO transition at 246 GHz shows possible signs of blending with the CH$_3$OCHO (19-18) transition.

5$\sigma$ was chosen as the threshold for the centroid velocity maps because, as explored in the Appendix, this is the optimal s/n to model dynamic emission without dilution from surrounding emission.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Hot corino thermal sublimation origin for formaldehyde and methanol emission, rejected because the dust is optically thick and the CH3OH peak is spatially shifted from the protostars, favouring shock-induced non-thermal desorption.

evidence.quote: This evidence strongly favours the scenario in which the injection of formaldehyde and methanol into the gas phase has occurred due to a shock as the observations appear to rule out the suggestion that A and/or B are hot corinos; indeed, (cite: vastel) found that the CH$_3$OH emission peak appears spatially shifted with respect to both sources.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Wing emission from the nearby strong H13CN (3-2) line or bandpass/continuum subtraction artefacts as the cause of the 0.1 K elevated baseline in HDCO 4(2,2)-3(2,1), rejected after re-cleaning a narrower velocity window excluding H13CN.

evidence.quote: The flatness of the spectrum seemed to be too consistent for any lines to be present, therefore, we postulated that this may be an effect of the wing emission of the nearby strong H$^{13}$CN transition. In order to check this, the spw was re-cleaned using the same method (the FAUST pipeline) but with a reduced velocity window excluding the H$^{13}$CN transition.
Thus, we conclude that the cause of the elevated baseline is most likely line emission of HDCO.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Infalling accretion streamer interpretation for the large-scale NW-SE dynamic H2CO feature, rejected because the velocity-distance relation is flat or outward rather than showing inward free-fall acceleration.

evidence.quote: However, due to a lack of a clear acceleration or deceleration, as well as a velocity relation that is flat or even outflowing, this investigation instead led to the conclusion that the feature is most likely not streamer-like in nature and, in fact, is most likely a second molecular outflow

limitations_admitted.value: Interferometric filtering may remove extended low-velocity emission near the systemic velocity.

evidence.quote: The interferometric nature of these observations does lead to the possibility that some low velocity CO emission may be filtered out, however, the region affected by this is spatially much more extended than the region where deuterated species are detected

limitations_admitted.value: The high-velocity component of HDCO 4(1,4)-3(1,3) at v_LSR >= 6 km s^-1 is blended with CH3OCHO 19(4,15)-18(4,14) A.

evidence.quote: a third component with v$\rm_{LSR}~\geq$ 6 km s$^{-1}$ that is affected by blending.
the most likely culprit is CH$_3$OCHO 19(4,15)-18(4,14) A, as illustrated in Fig. 8.

limitations_admitted.value: D2CO emission is weak, 2D deconvolution failed to converge, and its V_LSR (2.1 +/- 0.3 km s^-1) does not match any of the three H2CO/HDCO velocity components, preventing a firm constraint on the D2CO D/H ratio.

evidence.quote: This V$_{\rm LSR}$ value is not consistent with those obtained for H$_2$CO and HDCO, therefore it is unclear which of the three identified emission components this D$_2$CO emission corresponds to. Furthermore, due to the weakness of the emission, the 2D deconvolution failed to converge
Therefore, while we can use our results to obtain upper limit values for N$_{\rm TOT}$, we cannot constrain the D/H ratio for D$_2$CO with any kind of certainty.

limitations_admitted.value: The D/H calculation assumes uniform H2CO emission across the HDCO extraction polygon because spatial resolution is insufficient to resolve compact H2CO hotspots, making the derived D/H ratios upper limits.

evidence.quote: Despite this, it is worth noting that our D/H calculation assumes that the H$_2$CO emission is uniform across our extraction region where HDCO is emitting.

This means that compact H$_2$CO emission regions are also likely to exist, however our current resolution is insufficient to confirm this through direct observation. Therefore, to account for this, the D/H ratios for [BHB2007] 11 presented in this work are to be taken as upper limit values.

limitations_admitted.value: Present H2CO data alone cannot definitively establish the nature of the newly detected large-scale dynamic feature without additional molecular tracers.

evidence.quote: Therefore, while it is not possible with the present data alone to conclude on the nature of the dynamic material traced for the first time here, other molecular tracers detected towards these features would be very useful in contributing further evidence

referee_caveats_inferred: Only one undeuterated H2CO transition (E_u = 20.96 K) is observed and it suffers strong foreground self-absorption/envelope absorption between 2 and 5 km s^-1, overlapping the central 3.4 km s^-1 emission component and introducing substantial degeneracy into the H2CO column density and resulting D/H ratio.

H2CO is not corrected for beam dilution in Table 3 (unlike HDCO and D2CO, which are scaled for 0.15"-1.00" source sizes), which systematically underestimates N(H2CO) if H2CO is also compact and biases the D/H ratio upward (as the authors note when treating D/H as an upper limit).
Optical depth of the main isotopologue H2CO 3(0,3)-2(0,2) line in the compact disk components is not independently constrained via 13C isotopologues (H2^13CO).
